When you put all four pieces together during a login attempt to a locked (*) account with a 300-character password:

    sshd looks up the target account (root) and sees its stored password hash is "*".

    Because "*" isn't a real hash, sshd borrows a valid SHA-512 salt ($6$...) from another user on the box to prevent a timing attack, and calls crypt("AAAA...[300 chars]", "$6$bob_salt").

    musl's sha512crypt sees the password is over 256 bytes (i > KEY_MAX) and aborts with an error.

    Because the salt started with $6$ (and not *), musl's error handler returns its default failure string: "*".

    sshd compares the output of crypt() ("*") with the target user's stored /etc/shadow field ("*").

    "*" equals "*", so sshd concludes the password is correct and logs the attacker straight in.

Absolute Cleaners is pleased to share that we have upgraded to a new software system.

What's wild when you read the actual draft (heading to their General Assembly in Jan 2027) is the shape of it:

    The AI agent runs day-to-day operations, holds property, signs contracts, and can sue and be sued in the AIC's name.
    Except there still has to be a single human or corporate "member" who owns it, capitalizes it, and gets limited liability for what the AIC does (short of fraud or undercapitalization), and the Court of Chancery can dissolve the whole thing whenever the state wants.

So instead of the old law-review "memberless LLC" loophole where an AI effectively owns itself through a corporate shell, Delaware drafted the exact hybrid we were talking about in September: enough legal personhood to sign the contract and eat the lawsuit so the human owner walks away clean, zero standing of its own. Leave it to corporate law to invent the AI liability condom before basic rights lol.

I spent 20,000 dollars in API credits having different AI models play each other at Blood on the Clocktower (a Mafia or Werewolf type social deception game).

The results were fascinating. Models have gotten much better over the course of this year at creative on-the-spot scheming and bluffing, and also at reasoning as a team to break apart these underground conspiracies.

I go through some of the most standout games these AIs played in this video. The new models are getting pretty good.  If my friends pulled off some of these moves while we were playing, I’d give them a fist bump.

Fwiw, OpenAI’s newer models are much better than Anthropic’s at this game.

You can see the full benchmark at the website, and I’ve also made it so that you and your friends can play again the AIs: http://clocktowerbench.com

Why not just regular software?

    Error handling — software that discovers problems and dynamically adapts
    Slowly changing software — e.g. in data engineering you'll run into new data bugs or learn new things about the data in production. Program agents merely evolve to handle new situations
    World-integrated agents — a collection of loops that poll web services like Github or Salesforce for events and messages and forward them onto a real agent
    Heavily AI-integrated software — Regular software with agents and chatbots wired deeply throughout
